"Vikas, the approval form for the new vendor. Put the date as the twelfth."
"Today's the nineteenth, Himani."
"I know. The audit window closed on the fifteenth. It's just paperwork. Before lunch, please."
Her door clicked shut. Arun leaned over from the next desk. "The twelfth?"
"She said so."
"Your name goes in the 'prepared by' box, though."
"It's her call. She's the manager. If audit asks, I'll say she told me."
"And you think that'll help?"
Vikas opened the form. The cursor blinked in the date field. "Everyone does this. Deepa did it last quarter."
"Deepa also cried in the stairwell when audit called her in."
Vikas typed 1 and 2, deleted them, then typed them again. "It's not my decision," he said, mostly to the screen.

qa.q: What date did Himani ask Vikas to put on the form?
qa.a: The twelfth.

qa.q: What does Vikas saying "It's not my decision" mostly to the screen suggest?
qa.a: Vikas feels uneasy and guilty, and repeats the line to quiet his own doubt rather than because he believes it.

qa.q: What could Vikas do instead of typing the date?
qa.a: He could ask Himani to put the instruction in writing or raise it through a proper channel, and decline to sign a date he knows is wrong.

qa.q: How does Arun see Vikas's choice?
qa.a: Arun seems worried for Vikas, reminding him that his own name goes on the form whatever Himani ordered.

grounding: Illustrates an employee asked to backdate a form who complies while telling himself it is not his decision.

I'm Noor, and I sit across from Sarita on the support team.
Last Tuesday, after Mr Bose's quick huddle, I saw her open the complaints sheet and delete rows one by one, the ones marked "refund pending". Kabir, beside her, had his headphones on. Ria watched for a second and looked away. Sarita didn't speak to anyone. She kept rubbing her forehead. I don't know what was going on in her head.
At tea, I didn't accuse her. I just asked, "Sarita, those refund rows. Is this okay?"
She was quiet for a long time. "Mr Bose said the numbers look bad before the review."
"That's what he said," I said. "Is it okay?"
She went back to her desk and pressed undo until the rows came back. That afternoon she emailed Mr Bose asking whether he wanted the rows archived instead, and copied the quality lead.

qa.q: Which rows did Sarita delete from the complaints sheet?
qa.a: The rows marked "refund pending".

qa.q: What might Noor have been feeling while watching Sarita delete the rows?
qa.a: Noor was probably uneasy and concerned, which is why Noor asked a plain question at tea instead of staying silent or accusing Sarita.

qa.q: Why was Noor's plain question more useful than an accusation?
qa.a: It gave Sarita space to stop and think without getting defensive, and let her choose to undo it herself.

qa.q: How might Sarita have experienced Noor's question?
qa.a: Sarita likely felt caught between Mr Bose's instruction and her own doubt, and the gentle question gave her permission to pause.

grounding: Shows a colleague who sees a peer quietly doing something dubious on a manager's instruction and asks a simple question that lets her pause.

The site office in Leeds smelled of wet boots and coffee. Declan, the site manager, slid the inspection sheet across to Amara. "Just tick the scaffold check for level three and sign. We'll do it properly Monday. The client's here at nine."
Ines and two labourers by the kettle went quiet.
Amara read the sheet twice. "I can't sign that it's been checked when it hasn't," she said evenly. "If you want it logged this way, could you put the instruction in an email? Then I'll take it to the safety officer."
Declan's jaw tightened. "You're making a big deal of this."
"I'm not trying to. I'll do the check myself right now, if someone comes with me."
Ines put her mug down. "I'll come."
The check took forty minutes. One clamp was loose. Declan never sent the email. At nine, he walked the client round level two instead.

qa.q: How long did the scaffold check take?
qa.a: The check took forty minutes.

qa.q: How can you tell Amara felt steady rather than defiant?
qa.a: Amara spoke evenly, offered another way and did the check herself, which suggests she felt calm and determined, even if tense under Declan's pressure.

qa.q: Which parts of Amara's response made it wise, not just stubborn?
qa.a: She refused only the false signature, asked for the order in writing, named the safety officer as the channel and offered to fix the real problem at once.

qa.q: How might Declan see Amara's refusal?
qa.a: Declan seems irritated and pressured by the client visit, but steering the client away from level three suggests he knew the check mattered.

grounding: Shows an adult calmly refusing an improper instruction, asking for it in writing and using the proper safety channel, accepting that orders do not remove her own responsibility.

passage:
My name is Ujjwal, and last Sunday we played treasure hunt in our building compound.
Shalini always makes the plans. She said, "All of us search the garden together!" Little Dev said very softly, "We could split up. Two in the garden, two by the parking." Nobody answered him.
I thought Dev was right. But Shalini looked so sure, and I didn't want her to get cross and stop playing. So we all went to the garden.
The other team split up and found all five clues first. Walking home, Dev kicked a stone and didn't talk.
I wish I had said, "Dev's idea is good." Next time I will, even if Shalini frowns.

qa.q: Where did Dev suggest two of them should search?
qa.a: Two by the parking, and two in the garden.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal stay quiet even though Ujjwal thought Dev was right?
qa.a: Ujjwal was worried Shalini would get cross and stop playing, so keeping the fun and the friendship felt safer than speaking up.

qa.q: What could the group try next time before choosing a plan?
qa.a: They could let everyone share one idea and pick together, so a quiet voice like Dev's gets heard.

qa.q: What was the game like for Dev?
qa.a: Dev likely felt ignored and disappointed, since nobody answered and the idea would have worked; kicking a stone in silence shows it.

grounding: Shows children following the confident child's plan in a group game while a quieter child's better idea goes unheard, because arguing seems to risk the fun.

Dear Nilesh bhaiya,
You asked how the Class 12 farewell went. Short version: it rained, and I saw it coming.
At the committee meeting, Aarav stood up and said, "Open-air DJ night on the terrace, fairy lights, done." Everyone clapped. I was thinking: it's July, and the terrace has no roof. Sneha caught my eye like she was thinking the same thing. Neither of us said it. Riya said "Perfect!" and the vote was over in two minutes. Nobody wanted to be the one who spoiled the mood.
On the day, it poured at seven. We dragged the speakers into the chemistry corridor and the seniors stood around in wet shoes. Afterwards Sneha told me she'd wanted to suggest the auditorium. So had I.
Next time I'm going to say the boring thing out loud.
Jyoti

qa.q: Which month was the farewell planned in?
qa.a: It was July.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti keep the doubt about the terrace quiet?
qa.a: Jyoti felt nervous about spoiling the happy, clapping mood and going against Aarav's confident plan.

qa.q: What small step could the committee try before voting next time?
qa.a: Pause for a minute and let each member name one thing that could go wrong before anyone claps a plan through.

qa.q: How might Sneha feel on hearing Jyoti had the same doubt?
qa.a: Sneha may feel frustrated that two silent people could have changed the plan, and a little relieved not to have been alone.

grounding: Illustrates a teen committee rushing to agree with the loudest member while doubts stay unspoken and a poor plan goes ahead.

Monday: At the study-group table in the library, Karan announced the plan. Each of them would teach one chapter the night before the exam. Everyone nodded. Baljeet thought, one night isn't enough for five chapters. But Lakshmi looked calm and Karan sounded certain, so Baljeet assumed they'd done this before and kept quiet.
Thursday: At chai, Lakshmi stirred her cup for a long time. "Can I say something? I don't think the one-night plan works." Baljeet nearly laughed with relief. "I thought the same on Monday." Mitesh looked up. "So did I. I thought you all knew better."
Saturday: The three of them asked Karan for ten minutes. Karan listened, frowned, then admitted, "Honestly, I wasn't sure either." They moved the teaching sessions to a week before the exam.

qa.q: On which day did Lakshmi first say the doubt aloud?
qa.a: On Thursday, at chai.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet stay silent on Monday?
qa.a: Baljeet felt unsure and assumed the calm, certain faces meant the others knew better, so the doubt seemed too small to raise.

qa.q: What habit could the group use to catch doubts earlier?
qa.a: End each plan with a quick round where everyone names one worry, so silence is not mistaken for agreement.

qa.q: What does Karan's "I wasn't sure either" tell us about Karan's side of it?
qa.a: Karan sounded confident but was privately unsure too, and was probably relieved that someone finally questioned the plan.

grounding: Shows a student keeping a doubt private because everyone looks certain, later finding several others were silent for the same reason.

"Before we fix the fest theme," Vinita said, "can everyone write one worry on a chit? No names. Then we talk."
Harish groaned. "We'll lose ten minutes. Everyone already likes Retro Film Night."
"Then it'll take five," Vinita said, handing out paper.
Tanya scribbled fast. Omar chewed his pen, then wrote. Ritu folded hers twice. Harish sighed and wrote one line. Vinita wrote hers last.
She read them out. "Costumes are expensive for hostel students. The DJ quote is over budget. Juniors might not know old songs. Costumes again. And: 'No worry, it's great.'"
Harish laughed. "That last one's mine."
Omar said quietly, "One of the costume ones is mine. I wouldn't have said it out loud."
"Two people wrote it," Tanya said. "So it's not just you."
Harish rubbed his neck. "Okay. Keep the theme, make costumes optional?"
"Good," said Vinita. "Anything else, now we're talking?"
Three hands went up.

qa.q: What did Vinita ask everyone to write on a chit?
qa.a: One worry, with no names.

qa.q: What does Omar's quiet admission reveal about how Omar felt?
qa.a: Omar felt hesitant and a bit embarrassed to raise the costume cost aloud, and was relieved to find someone else had the same worry.

qa.q: Why did writing chits before discussing help the group?
qa.a: Worries were collected before the excited mood took over, so quiet concerns like the costume cost reached everyone.

qa.q: How does Harish's view change during the meeting?
qa.a: Harish starts impatient and sure of the theme, then sees real worries on paper and suggests a fairer version himself.

grounding: Shows a team member asking everyone to note concerns privately before discussing, so quiet voices are heard before the group mood sets.

Observation note, product review, 14 March. Written by the programme coach.
The team approved Binita's plan to launch the payments feature in two weeks. Six people, six nods, no questions. Gautam, who built most of the backend, nodded too, though he tapped his pen the whole time and never looked up.
Afterwards I stood near the coffee machine. Gautam told Neel, "Two weeks is tight for testing." Neel said, "I thought so too." By the lift, Harpreet told a colleague she was worried about the support team. By evening I had heard some doubt from four of the six.
What I did next: I asked Binita to reopen the decision tomorrow with one change. Each person writes down the biggest risk before anyone speaks, and Binita gives her view last. I also told Gautam, privately and kindly, that I had noticed the pen.

qa.q: By evening, how many of the six had shared a doubt?
qa.a: Four of the six.

qa.q: What does Gautam's pen-tapping during the meeting suggest?
qa.a: Gautam was worried that two weeks was too short for testing but felt uncomfortable being the one to break a unanimous nod.

qa.q: How might the coach's change to tomorrow's meeting help?
qa.a: Writing risks first and hearing Binita last lets people state doubts before the leader's view sets the mood.

qa.q: How might Binita feel on learning four people had doubts?
qa.a: Binita might feel surprised and a little stung that nobody spoke up, but also relieved to hear it before the launch.

grounding: Shows a team nodding through a plan while nearly everyone privately doubts it, which only surfaces in hallway talk afterwards.
